#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Stub-based tests for the deploy, backup, restore and post-receive scripts.
#
# systemctl, curl, sqlite3, git, npm, flock, ln and readlink are replaced with
# small stubs in a temporary directory, so this runs anywhere bash does.
# Run with: bash deploy/test/deploy.test.sh
set -euo pipefail

HERE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
DEPLOY="$HERE/../deploy.sh"
BACKUP="$HERE/../backup.sh"
RESTORE="$HERE/../restore.sh"
POST_RECEIVE="$HERE/../post-receive"

WORK="$(mktemp -d)"
cleanup() {
  rm -rf "$WORK"
}
trap cleanup EXIT

BIN="$WORK/bin"
LOG="$WORK/commands.log"
LINK_STATE="$WORK/current-link"
mkdir -p "$BIN"
: >"$LOG"
export WORK LOG LINK_STATE

cat >"$BIN/git" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "git $*" >>"$LOG"
if [ "${4:-}" = "add" ]; then mkdir -p "${5:?}"; fi
if [ "${4:-}" = "remove" ]; then rm -rf "${6:?}"; fi
exit 0
STUB

cat >"$BIN/npm" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "npm $*" >>"$LOG"
exit 0
STUB

cat >"$BIN/flock" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "flock $*" >>"$LOG"
exit 0
STUB

cat >"$BIN/systemctl" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "systemctl $*" >>"$LOG"
exit 0
STUB

cat >"$BIN/curl" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "curl $*" >>"$LOG"
if [ -f "$WORK/health-fail" ]; then
  exit 22
fi
printf '{"status":"ok"}\n'
STUB

cat >"$BIN/sqlite3" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "sqlite3 $*" >>"$LOG"
if [ "${2:-}" = "PRAGMA integrity_check;" ]; then
  if [ "${SQLITE3_BAD_INTEGRITY:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    echo "corrupt"
  else
    echo "ok"
  fi
  exit 0
fi
if [[ "${2:-}" == .backup* ]]; then
  if [ "${SQLITE3_BACKUP_FAIL:-0}" = "1" ]; then
    exit 1
  fi
  target="${2#.backup }"
  target="${target//\'/}"
  : >"$target"
  exit 0
fi
exit 0
STUB

cat >"$BIN/ln" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "ln $*" >>"$LOG"
printf '%s\n' "${2:-}" >"$LINK_STATE"
STUB

cat >"$BIN/readlink" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
echo "readlink $*" >>"$LOG"
if [ -f "$LINK_STATE" ]; then cat "$LINK_STATE"; fi
STUB

chmod +x "$BIN"/*
export PATH="$BIN:$PATH"

export APP_ROOT="$WORK/app"
export DB_PATH="$WORK/data/life.db"
export BACKUP_DIR="$WORK/backups"
export VERSION_FILE="$WORK/app/version.env"
export SERVICE_NAME="lifelogger"
export SYSTEMCTL="systemctl"
export CURL="curl"
export HEALTH_ATTEMPTS="2"
export HEALTH_DELAY="0"
export SUDO=""
export KEEP_RELEASES="5"

mkdir -p "$APP_ROOT" "$(dirname "$DB_PATH")"
printf 'APP_VERSION=v0.0.1\n' >"$VERSION_FILE"

PASSED=0
FAILED=0

pass() {
  PASSED=$((PASSED + 1))
  printf 'ok - %s\n' "$1"
}

fail() {
  FAILED=$((FAILED + 1))
  printf 'not ok - %s\n' "$1" >&2
}

assert_eq() {
  if [ "$1" = "$2" ]; then pass "$3"; else fail "$3 (expected [$2], got [$1])"; fi
}

assert_file_contains() {
  if grep -Fq -- "$2" "$1"; then pass "$3"; else fail "$3"; fi
}

assert_file_missing() {
  if grep -Fq -- "$2" "$1"; then fail "$3"; else pass "$3"; fi
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Successful deploy switches the current pointer and records the version.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
rm -f "$WORK/health-fail"
: >"$LOG"

if "$DEPLOY" v1.2.3 >"$WORK/deploy-ok.log" 2>&1; then
  pass "successful deploy exits zero"
else
  fail "successful deploy exits zero"
  cat "$WORK/deploy-ok.log" >&2
fi

assert_eq "$(cat "$LINK_STATE")" "$APP_ROOT/releases/v1.2.3" "current points at the new release"
assert_eq "$(cat "$VERSION_FILE")" "APP_VERSION=v1.2.3" "version file records the deployed tag"
assert_file_contains "$LOG" "npm ci" "deploy installs dependencies"
assert_file_contains "$LOG" "npm run build" "deploy builds the release"
assert_file_contains "$LOG" "systemctl restart lifelogger" "deploy restarts the service"
assert_file_contains "$LOG" "sqlite3" "deploy backs up the database when it exists"

# A second successful deploy moves the pointer again.
if "$DEPLOY" v1.2.4 >"$WORK/deploy-second.log" 2>&1; then
  pass "second deploy exits zero"
else
  fail "second deploy exits zero"
fi
assert_eq "$(cat "$LINK_STATE")" "$APP_ROOT/releases/v1.2.4" "second deploy points at its release"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# A failed health check rolls back to the previous release and version.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
touch "$WORK/health-fail"
: >"$LOG"

if "$DEPLOY" v1.2.5 >"$WORK/deploy-fail.log" 2>&1; then
  fail "failed health check exits non-zero"
else
  pass "failed health check exits non-zero"
fi

assert_eq "$(cat "$LINK_STATE")" "$APP_ROOT/releases/v1.2.4" "rollback restores the previous release"
assert_eq "$(cat "$VERSION_FILE")" "APP_VERSION=v1.2.4" "rollback restores the previous version"
assert_file_contains "$WORK/deploy-fail.log" "Rolled back" "rollback is reported"
if [ -d "$APP_ROOT/releases/v1.2.5" ]; then
  fail "failed release directory is removed"
else
  pass "failed release directory is removed"
fi
rm -f "$WORK/health-fail"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Invalid tags are rejected before any build or service change.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
: >"$LOG"
if "$DEPLOY" "v1.2" >"$WORK/deploy-bad.log" 2>&1; then
  fail "invalid tag is rejected"
else
  status=$?
  assert_eq "$status" "2" "invalid tag exits with status 2"
fi
assert_file_missing "$LOG" "npm" "invalid tag does not build"
assert_eq "$(cat "$LINK_STATE")" "$APP_ROOT/releases/v1.2.4" "invalid tag leaves current alone"

: >"$LOG"
if "$DEPLOY" "v1.2.3; echo pwned" >"$WORK/deploy-inject.log" 2>&1; then
  fail "tag with shell metacharacters is rejected"
else
  pass "tag with shell metacharacters is rejected"
fi
assert_file_missing "$LOG" "npm" "rejected tag does not build"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Dry run changes nothing.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
: >"$LOG"
if "$DEPLOY" v9.9.9 --dry-run >"$WORK/deploy-dry.log" 2>&1; then
  pass "dry run exits zero"
else
  fail "dry run exits zero"
fi
assert_file_contains "$WORK/deploy-dry.log" "Dry run" "dry run explains the plan"
assert_file_missing "$LOG" "npm" "dry run does not build"
assert_eq "$(cat "$LINK_STATE")" "$APP_ROOT/releases/v1.2.4" "dry run leaves current alone"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# post-receive deploys pushed v* tags only and ignores deletions and branches.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
cat >"$WORK/fake-deploy.sh" <<'STUB'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
printf '%s\n' "$1" >>"$WORK/deployed-tags"
STUB
chmod +x "$WORK/fake-deploy.sh"
: >"$WORK/deployed-tags"

printf 'old new refs/heads/main\nold new refs/tags/v1.2.6\nold %s refs/tags/v1.2.7\n' \
  "0000000000000000000000000000000000000000" |
  DEPLOY_SCRIPT="$WORK/fake-deploy.sh" "$POST_RECEIVE" >"$WORK/post-receive.log" 2>&1

assert_eq "$(cat "$WORK/deployed-tags")" "v1.2.6" "post-receive deploys only surviving v* tags"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Restore refuses to run without --yes, then restores a valid backup.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
backup_file="$WORK/restore-source.db"
printf 'backup contents\n' >"$backup_file"
printf 'live contents\n' >"$DB_PATH"
: >"$LOG"

if "$RESTORE" "$backup_file" >"$WORK/restore-refuse.log" 2>&1; then
  fail "restore without --yes is refused"
else
  status=$?
  assert_eq "$status" "3" "restore without --yes exits with status 3"
fi
assert_file_contains "$WORK/restore-refuse.log" "without --yes" "restore explains the confirmation"
assert_file_missing "$LOG" "systemctl stop" "refused restore does not stop the service"

if "$RESTORE" "$backup_file" --yes >"$WORK/restore.log" 2>&1; then
  pass "confirmed restore exits zero"
else
  fail "confirmed restore exits zero"
  cat "$WORK/restore.log" >&2
fi
assert_eq "$(cat "$DB_PATH")" "backup contents" "restore installs the chosen backup"
assert_file_contains "$LOG" "systemctl stop lifelogger" "restore stops the service"
assert_file_contains "$LOG" "systemctl start lifelogger" "restore starts the service"
if find "$WORK/data" -maxdepth 1 -name 'life.db.before-restore.*' | grep -q .; then
  pass "restore moves the live database aside"
else
  fail "restore moves the live database aside"
fi

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Backup writes a verified copy and fails on a corrupt copy.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
printf 'live contents\n' >"$DB_PATH"
rm -rf "$BACKUP_DIR"
: >"$LOG"

if "$BACKUP" >"$WORK/backup.log" 2>&1; then
  pass "backup exits zero"
else
  fail "backup exits zero"
  cat "$WORK/backup.log" >&2
fi

backup_copy="$(find "$BACKUP_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f -name 'life-logger-*.db' | head -n 1)"
if [ -n "$backup_copy" ]; then
  pass "backup creates a database copy"
else
  fail "backup creates a database copy"
fi
assert_file_contains "$LOG" "PRAGMA integrity_check;" "backup checks the copy"

if SQLITE3_BAD_INTEGRITY=1 "$BACKUP" >"$WORK/backup-bad.log" 2>&1; then
  fail "corrupt backup exits non-zero"
else
  pass "corrupt backup exits non-zero"
fi
if find "$BACKUP_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.tmp' | grep -q .; then
  fail "corrupt backup removes the temporary file"
else
  pass "corrupt backup removes the temporary file"
fi

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
printf '\n%d passed, %d failed\n' "$PASSED" "$FAILED"
if [ "$FAILED" -ne 0 ]; then
  exit 1
fi

# Life Logger deployment runbook

This folder is the complete server-side story: provisioning, systemd units, the
tag-triggered deploy, backups and restore. Read it before running anything on
the server. The owner reviews every file here first.

## Decisions to record before the first deploy

Fill these in as they are decided. They are repeated in the completion report.

| Decision | Value | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server OS | _pending_ | Run `findmnt /` and `lsblk -f`. If `/` is an `/run/archiso/cowspace` overlay, the machine is still the live installer; install Arch to the internal disk or record a written decision to accept the risk. |
| Repository visibility | Private (recommended) | A private repository keeps journal data models and host details out of public view. |
| Build location | Server first, PC fallback | A 3.8 GB Pentium may run out of memory during `npm ci` and the build. If it does, build on the PC and ship `node_modules` plus `dist` as the release artifact, and record why. |
| Device transport | _pending_ | A: HTTPS through Tailscale (preferred). B: allow cleartext HTTP for the Android app through Expo build properties. Record the choice here. |
| Node version | PC: v24.19.0, server: _pending_ | `node -v` on both. Match the major version before the first deploy. |
| Live vs installed OS | _pending_ | WP 3.5.4 step 1. Never deploy onto the live installer overlay. |

## Rules that keep releases safe

- **Migrations are additive within a release.** A release may add tables, columns
  and indexes. It must not drop or rewrite data that the previous release still
  needs. That is what makes rollback and a backup taken before deploy safe.
- **The database is backed up before `current` moves.** `deploy.sh` writes
  `/var/lib/lifelogger/backups/pre-<tag>.db` before switching the symlink.
- **A release is only live after `/health` passes.** A failed health check
  restores the previous symlink, version marker and service.
- **Secrets live in `/etc/lifelogger.env` only.** The repository never contains a
  password, private key, keystore or real API key.

## Paths

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/opt/lifelogger/repo.git` | Bare git repository; push tags here. |
| `/opt/lifelogger/releases/<tag>` | One built release per tag, pruned to the last 5. |
| `/opt/lifelogger/current` | Symlink to the live release. |
| `/opt/lifelogger/version.env` | `APP_VERSION=<tag>`, written by `deploy.sh`. |
| `/opt/lifelogger/deploy.sh`, `backup.sh`, `restore.sh` | Installed copies of the scripts in this folder. |
| `/var/lib/lifelogger/life.db` | Live SQLite database (WAL mode). |
| `/var/lib/lifelogger/backups` | Daily and pre-deploy backups, 14-day retention. |
| `/etc/lifelogger.env` | Runtime settings and the API key, mode 0640. |
| `/etc/systemd/system/lifelogger.service` | The application service. |
| `/etc/systemd/system/lifelogger-backup.{service,timer}` | Daily backup. |

## First install

1. **Check what the server is actually running.**
   ```bash
   findmnt /
   lsblk -f
   cat /etc/os-release
   node -v
   ```
   If `/` is an overlay under `/run/archiso/cowspace`, stop and install Arch to
   the internal disk first.

2. **SSH keys, password login off.**
   ```bash
   # on the PC
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "life-logger-server"
   ssh-copy-id <user>@<server>

   # on the server
   sudo sed -i 's/^#\?PasswordAuthentication .*/PasswordAuthentication no/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   sudo systemctl restart sshd
   ```

3. **Match Node.** Run `node -v` on the PC and the server. Install the same major
   version on the server if `pacman -S nodejs npm` does not provide it.

4. **Run the provisioning script from a checkout.**
   ```bash
   git clone <repository-url> ~/life-logger
   cd ~/life-logger
   sudo DEPLOY_USER="$USER" ./deploy/server-setup.sh
   ```
   The script is idempotent. It installs packages, creates the `lifelogger`
   service account, directories, zram swap, lid/sleep settings, units, a limited
   `sudoers` rule for service control, the bare repository and the hook. It also
   generates an API key in `/etc/lifelogger.env` the first time.

5. **Confirm the units.**
   ```bash
   systemctl is-enabled lifelogger.service lifelogger-backup.timer
   systemctl list-timers lifelogger-backup.timer
   ```

6. **Add the server remote and push.**
   ```bash
   # on the PC
   git remote add server <user>@<server>:/opt/lifelogger/repo.git
   git push server main
   git push server v0.3.5-increment-3.5
   ```
   Pushing the tag triggers `post-receive`, which runs `deploy.sh`.

7. **Verify.**
   ```bash
   curl -fsS http://<server>:8080/health
   curl -fsS http://<server>:8080/ | head
   sudo systemctl status lifelogger
   ```
   The web footer should show the same version as `/health`.

8. **Android.** Put the server address in the app's connection settings. For
   the emulator only, `http://10.0.2.2:4000` is the host alias. For a real phone,
   use the Tailscale name or LAN name. If cleartext HTTP is chosen, record that
   decision above; otherwise use HTTPS through Tailscale.

## Normal deploy

From the PC:

```bash
git tag v0.4.0-increment-4
git push server main --tags
```

The hook deploys only tags matching `v*`. Branch pushes and tag deletions are
ignored. Watch the push output; a failed health check makes the push fail and
the previous release comes back automatically.

Manual deploy (for example after re-running setup):

```bash
/opt/lifelogger/deploy.sh v0.4.0-increment-4
/opt/lifelogger/deploy.sh v0.4.0-increment-4 --dry-run
```

`deploy.sh` validates the tag against `^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[A-Za-z0-9._-]+)?$`,
takes an exclusive `flock`, builds in a private worktree, backs up the database,
moves `current`, restarts, health-checks for up to 10 seconds, rolls back on
failure and prunes releases beyond the last 5.

## Manual rollback

Automatic rollback happens when the health check fails. To roll back by hand:

```bash
ls -1dt /opt/lifelogger/releases/*
previous=/opt/lifelogger/releases/<previous-tag>
ln -sfn "$previous" /opt/lifelogger/current
printf 'APP_VERSION=%s\n' "$(basename "$previous")" > /opt/lifelogger/version.env
sudo systemctl restart lifelogger
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
```

Do not delete the bad tag before the rollback; keep it for the report, then
delete it from the server remote:

```bash
git push server :refs/tags/<bad-tag>
```

## Restore

Always take a fresh backup before a restore. `restore.sh` refuses to run without
`--yes` and refuses a backup that fails `PRAGMA integrity_check`.

```bash
sudo /opt/lifelogger/backup.sh
sudo /opt/lifelogger/restore.sh /var/lib/lifelogger/backups/<file>.db --yes
```

It stops the service, moves the live database to
`life.db.before-restore.<timestamp>`, removes stale `-wal`/`-shm` files, copies
the backup into place, starts the service and health-checks it. If the health
check fails, the script exits non-zero and points at `journalctl`.

For a **scratch restore drill**, restore to a temporary path first:

```bash
sudo DB_PATH=/tmp/life-logger-restore-drill.db \
  /opt/lifelogger/restore.sh /var/lib/lifelogger/backups/<file>.db --yes
sqlite3 /tmp/life-logger-restore-drill.db 'PRAGMA integrity_check;'
```

The service still stops and starts during this drill; it does not touch the
live database because `DB_PATH` is overridden.

## Backups

The timer runs daily at 03:30 with a 15-minute random delay and `Persistent=true`
(so a missed run catches up after boot). Each run:

1. Copies the live database with `sqlite3 .backup` (consistent while WAL is in use).
2. Runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` on the copy.
3. Keeps 14 days of `life-logger-*.db` files and exits non-zero on any failure.

```bash
sudo /opt/lifelogger/backup.sh
ls -lh /var/lib/lifelogger/backups
sqlite3 /var/lib/lifelogger/backups/<file>.db 'PRAGMA integrity_check;'
```

Backups on the same disk are lost with the disk. Copy them to the PC
periodically and record the date of the last copy:

```bash
scp '<user>@<server>:/var/lib/lifelogger/backups/*.db' ./backups/
```

## Logs and status

```bash
sudo systemctl status lifelogger
journalctl -u lifelogger -n 100 --no-pager
journalctl -u lifelogger -f
journalctl -u lifelogger-backup -n 50 --no-pager
systemctl list-timers lifelogger-backup.timer
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
```

`/health` returns `status`, `version`, `schemaVersion`, `syncProtocolVersion`,
`database` and `timestamp`. It uses a direct `SELECT 1` probe and never scans
application tables. A failure returns HTTP 503.

## Upgrading Node

1. Check the PC version: `node -v`.
2. On the server: `sudo pacman -Syu nodejs npm` (or install the matching version).
3. `sudo /opt/lifelogger/deploy.sh <current-tag> --dry-run` is not a build test;
   instead run the test suite from a release checkout:
   ```bash
   cd /opt/lifelogger/releases/<tag>
   npm ci
   npm test
   ```
4. Deploy the next tag normally. Record both Node versions in the report.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| `/health` returns 503 | `DB_PATH` in `/etc/lifelogger.env`, directory permissions, `journalctl -u lifelogger`. |
| Service will not start | `systemctl status lifelogger`, then `ls -l /opt/lifelogger/current`, `/opt/lifelogger/version.env`, and the Node path in the unit. |
| Push does not deploy | Tag must match `v*` and the regex above. Check `ls -l /opt/lifelogger/repo.git/hooks/post-receive` and run the deploy manually to see the error. |
| `deploy already running` | Another push is deploying. `flock` releases when the process exits; otherwise inspect `ps`. |
| Build runs out of memory | Confirm `zramctl` shows swap. Use the PC-build fallback and record the decision. Keep `MemoryMax=1G` on the service. |
| Native SQLite error | Node 24 ships `node:sqlite`; confirm the unit runs `/usr/bin/node` from the matched major version and that `node -e "require('node:sqlite')"` works. |
| Web shows an old version | Reload; `index.html` is `no-cache` and assets are hashed. Compare the footer with `/health`. |
| API returns 401 | The client's API key must equal `API_KEY` in `/etc/lifelogger.env`. |
| Phone cannot reach the server | Confirm Tailscale is up on both devices, the server address is set in the app, and the chosen HTTPS/cleartext option is built into the app. |
| Lock file after a crash | `flock` is advisory and released on process exit. Check `ps` before deleting `/opt/lifelogger/.deploy.lock`. |

## Verification drills

Record the date, result and timing for each.

1. **Rollback drill.** Push a throwaway tag whose build succeeds but health
   fails (for example, temporarily point `HEALTH_URL` at a bad path or start the
   service with a broken `DB_PATH`). Confirm the previous version returns.
2. **Restore drill.** Back up, change a marker, restore the backup with
   `restore.sh --yes`, confirm the data and `PRAGMA integrity_check`, and record
   the timing.
3. **Reboot drill.** `sudo reboot`, then confirm the service and backup timer
   return within 2 minutes without a login.
4. **Build drill.** Record `npm ci` plus build duration and peak memory, using
   `/usr/bin/time -v`, and the idle CPU/memory of the running service.

input.content:
# Life Logger

A personal, self-hosted system that records what you did and what state you were in, as an offline-first timeline of events and markers, enriched with context and free-text journaling.

Life Logger runs as a local web app on the PC, a React Native companion on Android, and a single-user Fastify service over SQLite. It is designed for one person, one database and no public internet exposure.

## Requirements

- Node.js 24 (tested with v24.19.0). Node 24 provides the built-in `node:sqlite` driver, so no native module build is required.
- npm 10 or newer.
- Linux with systemd for the always-on server. Development works on Windows, macOS or Linux.
- `bash` and `shellcheck` only if you want to run the deployment-script tests and lint locally.

## Install

```bash
git clone <repository-url> life-logger
cd life-logger
npm ci
```

`npm ci` installs every workspace: domain, persistence, sync, server, web, Android and the benchmark harness.

## Test

```bash
# Everything: domain, persistence, sync, server, Android logic and the bench CLI
npm test

# TypeScript project build (domain, persistence, sync, server and bench)
npm run typecheck

# Production build of the web app
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/web build

# Android type check
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/android exec tsc --noEmit

# Deployment scripts (bash, Linux or Git Bash)
npm run test:deploy
shellcheck deploy/*.sh deploy/post-receive deploy/test/*.sh
```

The server tests cover `/health` (ok and database failure), environment parsing, static web serving, API-key protection and graceful shutdown. The deploy test uses stubs for `systemctl`, `curl`, `sqlite3`, `git`, `npm`, `flock`, `ln` and `readlink`; it proves that a successful deploy moves the `current` pointer, that a failed health check rolls back, and that invalid tags are refused.

## Build

```bash
npm run build
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/web build
```

The server build outputs to `apps/server/dist`. The web build outputs to `apps/web/dist`, which the server serves directly.

## Run

Development, with two terminals:

```bash
# API on http://localhost:4000
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/server dev

# Web app on http://localhost:3000
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/web dev
```

Production-style local run:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
npm run build
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/web build
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/server start
# open http://localhost:4000
```

The server serves the built web app, falls back to `index.html` for client-side routes, and returns `no-cache` for `index.html` while hashed assets get a one-year immutable cache. The footer shows the version reported by `/health`.

Android companion:

```bash
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/android start
```

Set the server address in the app's connection settings. `http://10.0.2.2:4000` is the Android emulator alias for the development PC; a real phone needs the server's LAN or Tailscale name. See `deploy/README.md` for the HTTPS versus cleartext decision.

## Configuration

The server reads every setting from the environment. `.env.example` documents the same names. Development scripts load a root `.env` automatically through Node's `--env-file-if-exists`; the systemd unit loads `/etc/lifelogger.env` instead.

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DB_PATH` | `data/life-logger.sqlite` | SQLite database file. Relative paths resolve from the working directory. |
| `WEB_DIR` | `apps/web/dist` | Built web app directory. Static serving is skipped if it is missing. |
| `HOST` | `0.0.0.0` | Bind address. Use `127.0.0.1` behind a local reverse proxy. |
| `PORT` | `4000` | HTTP port. The server deployment uses `8080`. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | `fatal`, `error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug`, `trace` or `silent`. |
| `API_KEY` | unset | When set, every `/api/` request needs `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or `x-api-key`. `/health` and static files stay open. |
| `APP_VERSION` | root `package.json` version | Release identifier shown by `/health` and in the footer. |
| `DATA_DIR` | unset | Legacy convenience fallback: `DB_PATH` becomes `<DATA_DIR>/life-logger.sqlite`. |

`GET /health` is unauthenticated and returns:

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "database": "connected",
  "version": "v0.3.5-increment-3.5",
  "schemaVersion": 3,
  "syncProtocolVersion": 1,
  "timestamp": "2026-10-25T00:00:00.000Z"
}
```

The probe is a single `SELECT 1`; it does not scan application tables. A database failure returns HTTP 503.

## Repository layout

- [`packages/domain`](./packages/domain): Pure TypeScript domain entities (`Day`, `Marker`, `Event`, `Tag`, `Person`, `JournalEntry`, `Capture`, `Suggestion`), logical day resolution, timeline lanes and gap detection, derived day fidelity, deterministic quick-entry parsing, suggestion lifecycle rules, an ICS calendar parser, an extension registry, and Last-Write-Wins (LWW) conflict handling.
- [`packages/persistence`](./packages/persistence): Repository interfaces for days, markers, events, tags, people, journal entries, captures, suggestions and calendar metadata; SQLite (WAL mode) implementations; forward-only migrations and an engine-agnostic contract test suite.
- [`packages/sync`](./packages/sync): Outbox engine, batch push/pull protocol across all Daily Loop entity types plus suggestions, cursor-based synchronization and the sync protocol version.
- [`apps/server`](./apps/server): Node.js + Fastify API service with single-user authentication, runtime configuration, health reporting, graceful shutdown, static web serving, transactional sync ingestion, day timeline/gap endpoints, journal and end-of-day review endpoints, the suggestion inbox API, and the Calendar extension import endpoint.
- [`apps/web`](./apps/web): React + Vite web application with a multi-lane day timeline, gap detection, quick-entry capture, journal, end-of-day review modal, suggestion inbox, `.ics` calendar import, and a version footer.
- [`apps/android`](./apps/android): React Native / Expo companion app featuring quick-entry parsing, one-tap offline marker capture (< 50ms), a mini day timeline, offline review, an offline suggestion inbox with ICS paste import, automatic outbox synchronization, and a configurable server address.
- [`tools/bench`](./tools/bench): Synthetic dataset generator, benchmark harness, regression comparison and JSON output.
- [`scripts/`](./scripts): Local Windows backup and sandbox disaster-recovery helpers.
- [`deploy/`](./deploy): Arch provisioning, systemd units, tag-triggered deploy, backup, restore and the server runbook.
- [`docs/benchmarks`](./docs/benchmarks): Recorded benchmark baselines.
- [`docs/reports`](./docs/reports): Increment completion reports.

## Suggestions and the Calendar extension

Automated sources never write directly to the timeline. They propose items into the suggestion inbox, and only an explicit accept action creates an `Event` with `source = imported`:

1. Import an `.ics` file from the web suggestion inbox, or paste calendar text into the Android app while offline.
2. Each calendar `VEVENT` becomes a pending suggestion with `approx` times until you confirm it. UIDs are hashed into stable suggestion IDs so re-importing the same file is idempotent.
3. Accept, edit or reject each suggestion. Rejected items stay in storage, so a later import does not propose the same calendar item again.
4. Accepted calendar events also record module-owned metadata in `calendar_items` (external UID, recurrence rule, organizer and attendees) keyed by `event_id`.

Relevant API surface:

```text
GET    /api/v1/suggestions?status=pending
PATCH  /api/v1/suggestions/:suggestionId
POST   /api/v1/suggestions/:suggestionId/accept
POST   /api/v1/suggestions/:suggestionId/reject
GET    /api/v1/extensions
POST   /api/v1/extensions/calendar/import
```

Suggestion records synchronize through the existing outbox using the `suggestion` entity type. Accepting on Android works offline; the created event, accepted suggestion, and calendar metadata are reconciled when the device next syncs.

## Benchmarks

Build the harness once, then run it with an explicit output path and host label:

```bash
npm run --workspace=@life-logger/bench build

# PC baseline
node tools/bench/dist/index.js \
  --output docs/benchmarks/increment-3.5-pc-baseline.json \
  --host-label pc

# Server baseline, run from a release checkout on the server
node tools/bench/dist/index.js \
  --output docs/benchmarks/increment-3.5-server-baseline.json \
  --host-label server

# Regression guard: fail if any metric is more than 3x its baseline
node tools/bench/dist/index.js \
  --output /tmp/life-logger-bench.json \
  --host-label pc \
  --compare docs/benchmarks/increment-3.5-pc-baseline.json
```

The harness records CPU model, core count, total memory, Node version, platform, architecture, host label and app version alongside the 11 metric values and their pass/fail targets. Compare mode only checks metrics present in both files, so adding a metric does not break an older baseline. Any metric above its target, or more than three times its baseline, exits non-zero. Use `--help` for all options.

## Deployment

The always-on server runs the same code as a systemd service behind a tag-triggered deploy:

```bash
git tag v0.4.0-increment-4
git push server main --tags
```

`deploy/README.md` is the runbook: first install, server preparation, normal deploy, manual and automatic rollback, restore, backups, logs, Node upgrades, troubleshooting and the verification drills. The deploy scripts are shellcheck-clean and use stubs in tests, so the first real run is not the first run.

Secrets, private keys, keystores and real LAN addresses are never committed. Server settings belong in `/etc/lifelogger.env`, which the provisioning script creates with a generated API key.

### Connectivity through Tailscale

1. Install Tailscale on the server, the PC and the phone, and sign all three
   into the same tailnet:
   ```bash
   sudo pacman -S --needed tailscale
   sudo systemctl enable --now tailscaled
   sudo tailscale up
   tailscale status
   ```
2. Expose the service over HTTPS with a valid tailnet certificate:
   ```bash
   sudo tailscale serve --bg 8080
   tailscale serve status
   ```
   The app is then reachable at `https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net`. With this
   option set `HOST=127.0.0.1` in `/etc/lifelogger.env` so only Tailscale can
   reach the service, and restart the service.
3. On the phone, open that HTTPS URL in the Server Connection card. Android
   blocks plain HTTP by default, which is why option A needs no app build flag.
4. Option B, only if HTTPS is unavailable: allow cleartext for the app through
   Expo build properties, use `http://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net:8080`, and
   record that decision in the table above.
5. End-to-end check: log a marker on the PC and pull it on the phone, then
   reverse. Import an `.ics` file and confirm the suggestions reach the phone.

Do not forward port 8080 on the router. The service is for the tailnet only.

## Objective
- Complete Increment 3.5 of the Life Logger project: repository hygiene, runtime configuration/health, deployment artifacts, benchmark regression guard, and preparation for server deployment. It adds no product features.

## Requirements
- Follow `Increment 3.5 Repository, Server and Deployment.md` exactly; read existing scripts/config before naming things.
- Keep all earlier tests passing; new code gets tests.
- No secrets, passwords, private keys, keystores, or LAN addresses in the repository; use placeholders/environment variables.
- Prefer boring tools: bash, systemd, git, SQLite CLI. Add a runtime dependency only when necessary and explain why.
- Keep everything light for a Pentium T4300 / 3.8 GB RAM server. `/health` must not scan tables.
- No emojis in the UI.
- Destructive server actions require explicit owner confirmation.
- Shell scripts are Linux-targeted; add `.gitattributes` for LF. Mark scripts executable in git.
- When a step needs the owner, stop and list exactly what they must run.
- Out of scope: product features, schema changes/migrations, Android `expo-sqlite`, Diagnostics, search, things/types, recurring expansion, Docker, CI service, public internet exposure.

## Decisions
- Increment 3.5 is agent-side implementation first, then owner-only GitHub/server/Tailscale steps.
- Added `@fastify/static` for serving the built web app.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# One-time, idempotent provisioning for the Life Logger home server (Arch Linux).
#
# Installs packages and the service account, creates directories, configures
# zram and lid behaviour, installs the systemd units, and creates the bare git
# repository and post-receive hook. Safe to run more than once.
#
# Run from the repository checkout with sudo:
#   sudo DEPLOY_USER="$USER" ./deploy/server-setup.sh
set -euo pipefail

if [ "$(id -u)" -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Run this script as root (sudo)." >&2
  exit 1
fi

if [ ! -f /etc/arch-release ]; then
  echo "This script targets Arch Linux; /etc/arch-release was not found." >&2
  exit 1
fi

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"

APP_ROOT="${APP_ROOT:-/opt/lifelogger}"
DATA_DIR="${DATA_DIR:-/var/lib/lifelogger}"
ENV_FILE="${ENV_FILE:-/etc/lifelogger.env}"
SERVICE_NAME="${SERVICE_NAME:-lifelogger}"
DEPLOY_USER="${DEPLOY_USER:-${SUDO_USER:-lifelogger}}"
EXPECTED_NODE_MAJOR="${EXPECTED_NODE_MAJOR:-24}"

REPO="$APP_ROOT/repo.git"
RELEASES="$APP_ROOT/releases"
BACKUPS="$DATA_DIR/backups"

if ! id -u "$DEPLOY_USER" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Deploy user does not exist: $DEPLOY_USER (pass DEPLOY_USER=<name>)" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "== Packages =="
pacman -S --needed --noconfirm git nodejs npm sqlite3 curl zram-generator sudo

node_major="$(node -p 'process.versions.node.split(".")[0]')"
echo "Node $(node -v) installed (expected major: $EXPECTED_NODE_MAJOR)"
if [ "$node_major" != "$EXPECTED_NODE_MAJOR" ]; then
  echo "Warning: Node major $node_major differs from the PC's $EXPECTED_NODE_MAJOR." >&2
  echo "Match the PC version before the first deploy, or install it explicitly." >&2
fi

echo "== Service account =="
if ! id -u lifelogger >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  useradd --system --home-dir "$DATA_DIR" --create-home --shell /usr/bin/nologin lifelogger
  echo "Created lifelogger user"
else
  echo "lifelogger user already exists"
fi
usermod -aG lifelogger "$DEPLOY_USER"

echo "== Directories =="

164: `deploy.sh` validates the tag against `^v[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[A-Za-z0-9._-]+)?$`,
165: takes an exclusive `flock`, builds in a private worktree, backs up the database,

169: ## Manual rollback
170: 
171: Automatic rollback happens when the health check fails. To roll back by hand:
172: 
173: ```bash
174: ls -1dt /opt/lifelogger/releases/*
175: previous=/opt/lifelogger/releases/<previous-tag>
176: ln -sfn "$previous" /opt/lifelogger/current
177: printf 'APP_VERSION=%s\n' "$(basename "$previous")" > /opt/lifelogger/version.env
178: sudo systemctl restart lifelogger
179: curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
180: ```
181: 
182: Do not delete the bad tag before the rollback; keep it for the report, then
183: delete it from the server remote:
184: 
185: ```bash
186: git push server :refs/tags/<bad-tag>
187: ```

189: ## Restore
190: 
191: Always take a fresh backup before a restore. `restore.sh` refuses to run without
192: `--yes` and refuses a backup that fails `PRAGMA integrity_check`.
193: 
194: ```bash
195: sudo /opt/lifelogger/backup.sh
196: sudo /opt/lifelogger/restore.sh /var/lib/lifelogger/backups/<file>.db --yes
197: ```
198: 
199: It stops the service, moves the live database to
200: `life.db.before-restore.<timestamp>`, removes stale `-wal`/`-shm` files, copies
201: the backup into place, starts the service and health-checks it. If the health
202: check fails, the script exits non-zero and points at `journalctl`.
203: 
204: For a **scratch restore drill**, restore to a temporary path first:
205: 
206: ```bash
207: sudo DB_PATH=/tmp/life-logger-restore-drill.db \
208:   /opt/lifelogger/restore.sh /var/lib/lifelogger/backups/<file>.db --yes
209: sqlite3 /tmp/life-logger-restore-drill.db 'PRAGMA integrity_check;'
210: ```
211: 
212: The service still stops and starts during this drill; it does not touch the
213: live database because `DB_PATH` is overridden.
214: 
215: ## Backups
216: 
217: The timer runs daily at 03:30 with a 15-minute random delay and `Persistent=true`
218: (so a missed run catches up after boot). Each run:
219: 
220: 1. Copies the live database with `sqlite3 .backup` (consistent while WAL is in use).
221: 2. Runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` on the copy.
222: 3. Keeps 14 days of `life-logger-*.db` files and exits non-zero on any failure.
223: 
224: ```bash
225: sudo /opt/lifelogger/backup.sh
226: ls -lh /var/lib/lifelogger/backups
227: sqlite3 /var/lib/lifelogger/backups/<file>.db 'PRAGMA integrity_check;'
228: ```

231: periodically and record the date of the last copy:
232: 
233: ```bash
234: scp '<user>@<server>:/var/lib/lifelogger/backups/*.db' ./backups/
235: ```

238:

240: sudo systemctl status lifelogger
241: journalctl -u lifelogger -n 100 --no-pager
242: journalctl -u lifelogger -f
243: journalctl -u lifelogger-backup -n 50 --no-pager
244: systemctl list-timers lifelogger-backup.timer
245: curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health
246: ```

248: `/health` returns `status`, `version`, `schemaVersion`, `syncProtocolVersion`,
249: `database` and `timestamp`. It uses a direct `SELECT 1` probe and never scans
250: application tables. A failure returns HTTP 503.

254: 1. Check the PC version: `node -v`.

267: | Symptom | Check |
268: | --- | --- |
269: | `/health` returns 503 | `DB_PATH` in `/etc/lifelogger.env`, directory permissions, `journalctl -u lifelogger`. |

277: | Phone cannot reach the server | Confirm Tailscale is up on both devices, the server address is set in the app, and the chosen HTTPS/cleartext option is built into the app. |

# Increment 3.5: Repository, Server and Deployment — Completion & Verification Report

> **Project:** Life Logger  
> **Milestone:** Increment 3.5 (repository hygiene, runtime configuration, deployment)  
> **Git Release Tag:** `v0.3.5-increment-3.5`  
> **Date:** October 25, 2026  
> **Status:** Agent-side engineering complete — every automated gate passed locally. GitHub publication, server provisioning, the real drills and dual-device sync remain owner actions.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Increment 3.5 adds no product behaviour. It turns a working codebase into something that can be cloned, configured, deployed, backed up, rolled back and measured without guesswork:

- The repository has no secrets, no absolute `file:///C:/Users/...` links (in the working tree *or* in history), LF endings for shell scripts, and executable bits recorded in git.
- The server reads all runtime settings from environment variables, exposes `/health` with version, schema version, sync protocol version and a single-row database probe, serves the built web app, and shuts down cleanly on `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`.
- `deploy/` contains a complete Arch Linux story: idempotent provisioning, systemd units, tag-triggered deploy with pre-deploy backup and automatic rollback, daily backups with integrity checks, a guarded restore, and a runbook.
- The benchmark harness gains host details, JSON output, a PC/server label and a 3x regression comparison, so the server baseline can be compared against the PC baseline without hand-editing JSON.
- The owner confirmed the server runs Arch Linux. The provisioning script already targets Arch and refuses to run elsewhere.

The remaining work needs the GitHub repository, the physical server and the phone. Section 12 lists the exact commands.

---

## 2. Delivered Work Packages

| WP | Deliverable | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **WP 3.5.1** | Repository hygiene: secret scan, relative links, `.gitattributes`, executable scripts, history rewrite | Complete (agent) |

---

## 3. Architecture and Key Files

### Runtime configuration (`apps/server/src/config.ts`)

Every setting comes from the environment, with development defaults:

| Variable | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `DB_PATH` | `data/life-logger.sqlite` (or under `DATA_DIR`) | SQLite file; relative paths resolve against the working directory. |
| `WEB_DIR` | `apps/web/dist` | Built web app served by the API process. |
| `HOST` | `0.0.0.0` | Bind address. Use `127.0.0.1` behind Tailscale Serve. |
| `PORT` | `4000` | HTTP port. |
| `LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | `fatal` through `silent`; invalid values stop startup. |
| `API_KEY` | unset | When set, every `/api/` request needs `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. |
| `APP_VERSION` | root `package.json` version | Release identifier; deploys set it from the tag. |
| `DATA_DIR` | `data` | Local-development fallback when `DB_PATH` is unset. |

`.env.example` documents the same names. `npm run dev` and `npm start` load the root `.env` with `--env-file-if-exists`, so a Windows developer does not need to export variables by hand.

The schema version is read once at startup, not per request. `/health` therefore never scans application tables.

### Health, static serving and shutdown

`GET /health` returns:

```json
{
  "status": "ok",
  "database": "connected",
  "version": "v0.3.5-increment-3.5",
  "schemaVersion": 3,
  "syncProtocolVersion": 1,
  "timestamp": "2026-10-25T…Z"
}
```

The probe is `SELECT 1`; a database failure returns HTTP 503 with `status: "error"` and `database: "unavailable"`. `/health` and the static assets stay open; the API key hook is scoped to `/api/`.

The built web app is served by the same process through `@fastify/static`. `index.html` is `no-cache`, hashed assets are `immutable`, and unknown extension-less `GET` paths fall back to `index.html` for client-side routing. `/api/`, `/health` and missing files still return JSON 404s.

`@fastify/static` is the only new runtime dependency. The alternative — a second static server or a reverse proxy — would add another process and more RAM to a 3.8 GB machine. The web app is already built by Vite; serving it from Fastify keeps one process and one port.

`SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` stop accepting requests, drain in-flight work, run `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`, close SQLite and exit 0 (1 on failure). Repeated signals are ignored, and a 10-second guard forces exit if a close hangs.

### Sync protocol

`SYNC_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1` now lives in `packages/sync/src/protocol.ts` and is reported by `/health`, so a client can detect a server that speaks an older protocol before syncing.

### Web and Android

- The web footer fetches `/health` and shows the deployed version.
- Android has a **Server Connection** card for the server URL and API key, with a test for the client accessors. The values live for the current app session; durable settings arrive with `expo-sqlite` in Increment 4.

### Benchmark tooling

`tools/bench` gained `--output`, `--host-label`, `--compare` and `--help`. Output records CPU model, core count, RAM, Node version, platform, architecture and app version. `--compare <baseline>` fails when any shared metric exceeds 3x its baseline value, and prints the ratio. New metrics do not fail against an older baseline.

1. A mirror backup was taken at `C:\Users\thema\AppData\Local\Temp\opencode\you-backup.git`.
2. `git filter-branch --tree-filter` ran the link fixer over every commit, with `--tag-name-filter cat -- --all`.

There are no other clones, so no collaborator needs to re-clone. The mirror backup is deleted once the owner is satisfied with the GitHub push.

### Line endings and executable bits

`.gitattributes` forces LF for `*.sh`, `*.service`, `*.timer` and everything under `deploy/`, keeps CRLF for PowerShell, and treats database and image files as binary. `deploy.sh`, `backup.sh`, `restore.sh`, `server-setup.sh`, `post-receive` and the deploy test are recorded as mode `100755` in git.

## 5. Deployment Design

| Piece | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `server-setup.sh` | Refuses non-Arch hosts (`/etc/arch-release`). Installs `git nodejs npm sqlite3 curl zram-generator sudo`, creates the `lifelogger` service account, directories, zram, lid settings, units, a narrow `systemctl` sudoers rule, the bare repository and the hook. Idempotent. |
| `post-receive` | Deploys only tags matching `v*`; branch pushes and tag deletions are ignored. |
| `deploy.sh` | Validates the tag regex, takes a `flock`, builds in a private worktree, backs up the database, switches `current`, writes `version.env`, restarts the service, health-checks for 10 seconds and rolls back on failure. Keeps the last five releases. Supports `--dry-run`. |
| `lifelogger.service` | Runs as `lifelogger`, reads `/etc/lifelogger.env`, sets `MemoryMax=1G`, restarts on failure, and stops gracefully. |
| `backup.sh` + timer | `sqlite3 .backup`, `PRAGMA integrity_check` on the copy, 14-day retention, non-zero exit on any failure. Daily at 03:30 with a 15-minute jitter and `Persistent=true`. |
| `restore.sh` | Refuses without `--yes`, refuses a backup that fails integrity, stops the service, moves the live database aside, clears `-wal`/`-shm`, copies the backup, starts the service and health-checks. `DB_PATH` can point at a scratch file for the drill. |

Deploys run as the owner's account (`DEPLOY_USER`, default `${SUDO_USER}`); the service and data are owned by `lifelogger`. The repository and releases are owned by the deploy user, so `git push` and builds do not need broad sudo.

39: ## 3. Architecture and Key Files
40: 
41: ### Runtime configuration (`apps/server/src/config.ts`)
42: 
43: Every setting comes from the environment, with development defaults:
44: 
45: | Variable | Default | Purpose |
46: |---|---|---|
47: | `DB_PATH` | `data/life-logger.sqlite` (or under `DATA_DIR`) | SQLite file; relative paths resolve against the working directory. |
48: | `WEB_DIR` | `apps/web/dist` | Built web app served by the API process. |
49: | `HOST` | `0.0.0.0` | Bind address. Use `127.0.0.1` behind Tailscale Serve. |
50: | `PORT` | `4000` | HTTP port. |
51: | `LOG_LEVEL` | `info` | `fatal` through `silent`; invalid values stop startup. |
52: | `API_KEY` | unset | When set, every `/api/` request needs `Authorization: Bearer <key>`. |
53: | `APP_VERSION` | root `package.json` version | Release identifier; deploys set it from the tag. |
54: | `DATA_DIR` | `data` | Local-development fallback when `DB_PATH` is unset. |
55: 
56: `.env.example` documents the same names. `npm run dev` and `npm start` load the root `.env` with `--env-file-if-exists`, so a Windows developer does not need to export variables by hand.
57: 
58: The schema version is read once at startup, not per request. `/health` therefore never scans application tables.
59: 
60: ### Health, static serving and shutdown
61: 
62: `GET /health` returns:
63: 
64: ```json
65: {
66:   "status": "ok",
67:   "database": "connected",
68:   "version": "v0.3.5-increment-3.5",
69:   "schemaVersion": 3,
70:   "syncProtocolVersion": 1,
71:   "timestamp": "2026-10-25T…Z"
72: }
73: ```
74: 
75: The probe is `SELECT 1`; a database failure returns HTTP 503 with `status: "error"` and `database: "unavailable"`. `/health` and the static assets stay open; the API key hook is scoped to `/api/`.
76: 
77: The built web app is served by the same process through `@fastify/static`. `index.html` is `no-cache`, hashed assets are `immutable`, and unknown extension-less `GET` paths fall back to `index.html` for client-side routing. `/api/`, `/health` and missing files still return JSON 404s.
78: 
79: `@fastify/static` is the only new runtime dependency. The alternative — a second static server or a reverse proxy — would add another process and more RAM to a 3.8 GB machine. The web app is already built by Vite; serving it from Fastify keeps one process and one port.
80: 
81: `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` stop accepting requests, drain in-flight work, run `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`, close SQLite and exit 0 (1 on failure). Repeated signals are ignored, and a 10-second guard forces exit if a close hangs.
82: 
83: ### Sync protocol
84: 
85: `SYNC_PROTOCOL_VERSION = 1` now lives in `packages/sync/src/protocol.ts` and is reported by `/health`, so a client can detect a server that speaks an older protocol before syncing.

88: 
89: - The web footer fetches `/health` and shows the deployed version.
90: - Android has a **Server Connection** card for the server URL and API key, with a test for the client accessors. The values live for the current app session; durable settings arrive with `expo-sqlite` in Increment 4.
91: 
92: ### Benchmark tooling
93: 
94: `tools/bench` gained `--output`, `--host-label`, `--compare` and `--help`. Output records CPU model, core count, RAM, Node version, platform, architecture and app version. `--compare <baseline>` fails when any shared metric exceeds 3x its baseline value, and prints the ratio. ## Objective
- Complete Increment 3.5 of the Life Logger project (repository hygiene, runtime config/health, deployment artifacts, benchmark guard) and publish it to the existing GitHub repository.
- The server is Arch Linux (owner-confirmed); remaining work is server provisioning, first deploy, drills and Tailscale/Android sync.

## Requirements

- No secrets, passwords, private keys, keystores or LAN addresses in the repo or its history; use placeholders/env vars.

- `/health` must not scan application tables; light for Pentium T4300 / 3.8 GB RAM.
- No emojis in the UI; shell scripts Linux-targeted, LF endings, executable bits in git.

- Graceful shutdown: 10s guard, WAL checkpoint `TRUNCATE`, close SQLite, exit 0/1, ignore repeated signals.

### Accepted risk: persistent archiso server

The owner was shown the evidence below and chose, in writing on 2026-10-26, to run
Life Logger on the persistent archiso environment rather than reinstall Arch to
the internal disk. Reinstalling cannot be done over SSH because the running
overlay's writable layer is on the disk that would be formatted.

Evidence collected on `zeserver` (Tailscale MagicDNS, `root@zeserver`):

```text
/            airootfs  overlay  upperdir=/run/archiso/cowspace/persistent_/x86_64/upperdir
/run/archiso/cowspace  ext4  /dev/sda2  label SERVER_DATA
/dev/sda1    4G   vfat   ARCH_BOOT
loop0        854M squashfs /run/archiso/airootfs
kernel       7.2.6-arch2-1
cmdline      archisobasedir=arch archisosearchuuid=2025-06-01-09-10-39-00 copytoram=y cow_label=SERVER_DATA
firmware     Legacy BIOS (no /sys/firmware/efi)
fstab        empty
packages     762, including linux 7.2.11.arch1-1 (not the running kernel)
```

What this means in practice:

- Installed packages, `/etc`, `/home` and the database survive reboots, because the
  overlay's writable layer is the ext4 partition on `sda2`.
- The boot chain uses the **ISO's** kernel and initramfs on `sda1`, not the `linux`
  package's. The installed `linux` package is therefore not what boots the machine.
- There is no `fstab` and no installed bootloader configuration to rebuild; the
  machine is only recoverable through the archiso boot entry and the ISO.

Mitigations that go with the acceptance:

1. **No blind full upgrades.** `pacman -Syu` can pull a `linux` package whose
   modules no longer match the ISO kernel. Upgrade deliberately, reboot, and
   re-run `systemctl is-active lifelogger lifelogger-backup.timer` plus `/health`.
2. **Keep the ISO and its boot entry.** Recovery depends on booting the same
   `archisosearchuuid=2025-06-01-09-10-39-00` with `cow_label=SERVER_DATA`.
   Copy the ISO somewhere off the machine and record its name and checksum here.
3. **Watch the overlay.** `df -h /` reports the writable layer. At acceptance:
   18 GiB of 114 GiB used, 91 GiB free. A full overlay breaks writes and the app.
4. **Off-machine copies.** Weekly copy of `/var/lib/lifelogger/backups`, `/etc`,
   and `pacman -Qqe` to the PC. The server has no second disk.
5. **No unattended kernel or security updates.** This is a home server on a
   tailnet, not an internet-facing host; the app still binds per `/etc/lifelogger.env`.

If the machine is ever reinstalled properly, `server-setup.sh` is idempotent and
the decision above can be replaced with the installed-system facts.

The user interrupted and asks: "stop; why not make it a nice pacman package and set it up as a systemd service?"

They're proposing packaging Life Logger as a pacman package and running it as a systemd service. Note: we already have a systemd service (lifelogger.service) installed and enabled from the deploy setup — it runs the app from /opt/lifelogger/current. So part of the question is already true. But they may mean: instead of the git-tag deploy pipeline, build a proper Arch package (PKGBUILD, .pkg.tar.zst) installing to /usr/lib/lifelogger, config in /etc, service unit owned by the package, and install/upgrade with pacman.

I should:
1. Stop the current work (they said stop). Confirm I stopped the SSH diagnostics; check whether a remote mount is left behind (/mnt/archboot may still be mounted since the timed-out command didn't unmount). I should clean that up — it's a leftover side effect. That's a quick, safe remote command. But they said stop... cleaning up a mount I created is responsible and low-risk. I'll do it and mention it.

2. Answer the design question honestly: tradeoffs between the current tag-deploy pipeline and a pacman package.

Arguments for pacman package:
- Arch-native: pacman owns files, upgrades via pacman -U, clean uninstall, dependency metadata, no custom deploy script.
- Service unit can ship in the package (/usr/lib/systemd/system/lifelogger.service), /etc/lifelogger.env as backup file.
- Build once, install everywhere; reproducible builds with makepkg.
- On this archiso setup, pacman is the natural update path... but wait, this is precisely where it's dangerous: the live env's pacman is already fragile (kernel/modules mismatch). Adding an app package doesn't change that.

Arguments against / complications:
- The repo currently deploys a *built* artifact (web dist + server dist) via git tag. A package would need to build from source at package build time (makedepends nodejs/npm), producing a .pkg.tar.zst. That's a real shift in release engineering: PKGBUILD, source tarball from the git tag, offline npm ci, reproducible-ish, signature.
- Node app packaging conventions: install JS to /usr/lib/lifelogger, symlink /usr/bin/lifelogger, systemd unit, /etc/lifelogger.env (backup=), /var/lib/lifelogger owned by a system user created via sysusers.d, tmpfiles.d. That is genuinely nicer than /opt + symlink releases.
- But: node_modules for a monorepo including Expo/React Native is huge; packaging only the server + web workspaces needs a production-only install, which npm workspaces make awkward (npm ci --workspace server --omit=dev still installs root deps?). Need pruning. Could use `npm ci --omit=dev` then remove android/web build deps; or bundle server with esbuild into a single JS file (best for a small package, avoids node_modules entirely). That's a bigger change.
- Versioning: package version from tag (0.3.5), pkgrel bumps for packaging-only changes.
- Rollback with pacman: downgrade by installing the previous .pkg.tar.zst; keep old packages in a local repo. `pacman -U` works offline. Simpler than symlink releases? Arguably yes: one command, and pacman tracks file ownership.
- Database and config survive upgrades because they're not package-owned (data in /var/lib, config in /etc with backup).
- Signing: for a personal server, unsigned local package is fine; optionally sign with a local key.
- The current pipeline's advantages: zero packaging knowledge, health-check + auto-rollback built in, works from Windows, deploys in one git push. A pacman package needs makepkg on the server (or cross-build in a container), and auto-rollback is manual (pacman -U previous).
- Scope: Increment 3.5 spec explicitly chose deploy.sh/tag push; switching now is a scope change to Increment 4+ and would invalidate the workflow just verified (37 deploy tests). The user is the owner and can change scope, but I should point out the cost.

Given they asked "why not", the honest answer: it's a reasonable idea with real benefits, and a real cost; it doesn't replace the systemd service (already there) but replaces the deploy mechanism. Recommend: finish getting v0.3.5 running now via the existing pipeline (it's minutes away), then do packaging as its own work package (WP 4.x) with a PKGBUILD + local repo, keeping the same systemd unit and env file. Or, if they prefer, switch now and I'll build the PKGBUILD first — but the app still needs a working health check and data dir, and we'd be debugging packaging and first-deploy simultaneously.

Also important: the immediate finding — the machine's boot chain is stale and zram can't work; the reboot drill is risky. The user said stop before I finished diagnosing. I must flag that: do not reboot until the sda1 kernel/initramfs sync is understood; currently sda1 has 7.2.6-ish kernel dated Sep 17 (vmlinuz 17MB Sep 17, initramfs 245MB Sep 17) and the ISO's 6.14.9 copies. Running 7.2.6 with /lib/modules/7.2.11 only. So a reboot would boot the Sep 17 7.2.6 kernel from sda1 (fine, presumably), modules still missing → zram broken. To fix, copy the current /boot/vmlinuz-linux (7.2.11) + initramfs to sda1. But that must be validated (archiso hook must be present in the initramfs, since it needs to find the squashfs).

Interesting: overlay /boot/vmlinuz-linux strings gave "unknown" because `strings` on a compressed bzImage may not find "Linux version" (it's in setup header, should be plain text though). Whatever.

Big change, and a good one — but three decisions determine the whole shape, and one of them is a real constraint on this PC.

**Constraint first:** `makepkg` does not run on Windows natively. "Compilation on this PC" works fine for the app (npm ci, tsc, Vite, esbuild), but assembling a valid `.pkg.tar.zst` needs a Linux-style toolchain. Your WSL is currently broken (`Failed to attach disk … ext4.vhdx`), so the realistic choices are:

- **A.** Build the JS artifacts here, then assemble the package with a Node script using Windows' bundled `bsdtar` plus `zstd.exe` (winget install). Writes `.PKGINFO`, `.MTREE`, sets modes, produces a package pacman accepts. No WSL, no Docker, stays on this PC.
- **B.** Repair/reinstall WSL and run real `makepkg` inside it. More "correct", but it means fixing WSL and using an Arch container, which is more than the task needs.
- **C.** Assemble on the server anyway (contradicts your instruction, but it is the least new machinery).

Second decision is distribution: a GitHub **Release asset per version** (`pacman -U <url>`, plus a small updater) versus a real **pacman repo on GitHub Pages** (`repo-add`, add one `Server =` line, then `pacman -Sy lifelogger` and ordinary upgrades). The Pages repo is the "nice pacman package" experience; the release asset is fewer moving parts and keeps binaries out of git history.

Third is versioning: map the existing `v0.3.5-increment-3.5` tag to `pkgver=0.3.5`, or switch tags to plain `v0.3.5` and let `pkgrel` carry packaging-only bumps.

options.label: Node + bsdtar + zstd on PC (Recommended)
options.description: Build JS artifacts on this PC, then a small Node packager writes .PKGINFO/.MTREE and compresses with zstd. Cross-platform, no WSL, no Docker; the output is verified by installing it on the server.

options.description: Fix the broken WSL distro, run makepkg in an Arch environment. Most orthodox packaging path, but adds WSL repair and a container/chroot to the work.

options.label: Assemble on the server
options.description: Build the app on this PC, ship the built tree, and run makepkg on zeserver. Simplest tooling, contradicts the compile-on-PC requirement.

options.label: Release asset + updater (Recommended)
options.description: Each tag gets a GitHub Release with lifelogger-<ver>-1-x86_64.pkg.tar.zst. Install/upgrade with a small lifelogger-update helper that resolves the latest release, runs pacman -U, health-checks and downgrades on failure.

options.label: Pacman repo on GitHub Pages
options.description: repo-add a lifelogger.db on a gh-pages branch; the server adds one Server = line and uses pacman -Sy / -Syu for real upgrades. Nicer UX, but binaries live in git and the repo needs rebuilding on every release.
